#2506. Karl and Laimer on target as Bayern Munich cruise past Atlético Madrid

Looking to get back to winning ways in Europe after drawing 1-1 with Stuttgart last time out, Atlético Madrid made a lively start as Bayern visited the Metropolitano, with talisman Julian Alvarez curling an effort narrowly wide of Manuel Neuer's far post inside three minutes.

Bayern then quickly took control, but despite enjoying over 70 per cent of the ball in the opening 20 minutes, they failed to register a shot, while Atléti midfielder Pablo Barrios saw a deflected effort fly just over.

Lennart Karl threatened midway through the half, firing over from the edge of the box, while Kane put an effort just wide following a delivery from Konrad Laimer.

On the half-hour mark, the hosts should have taken the lead, with Alexander Sørloth handed a chance he will not want to see again, with the Norwegian unable to sort his feet out following a ball to the back stick from Marc Pubill.

And after both sides failed to manage a shot on target before the break, Joshua Kimmich finally tested Jan Oblak shortly after the restart, before Karl broke the deadlock in the 54th minute.

Robin Le Normand appeared to have the ball under control near the penalty spot after blocking an effort from Tom Bischof, but the youngster then stole possession from behind the Spanish defender and fired the visitors into the lead.

Koke, Ademola Lookman and Lee Kang-in would come on for the hosts five minutes later, and Los Colchoneros began to find their feet after the changes, with Marcos Llorente forcing Neuer into his first save of the evening in the 67th minute.

Goalscorer Karl was replaced by Nathaniel Brown shortly afterwards, before Kane went close to doubling Bayern's advantage, only for the flag to be raised after the England captain lifted an effort narrowly over after rounding the onrushing Oblak.

Bayern would double their lead in the 74th minute, when Laimer hammered in off the crossbar from a tight angle following a beautifully clipped ball from Kane.

In the ascendancy and carrying a two-goal lead, the record German champions were well on track to pick up their first Champions League win since the opening week triumph against Bodø/Glimt.

Bayern did think they had a third in the 82nd minute, when Dayot Upamecano headed home from a corner, before the effort was ruled out for a foul, and left-back Brown then had a chance to extend the lead, only to be denied by Oblak on the angle.

Seeing out the win, Bayern take three points back to Munich with them and turn their European form back around after successive draws, while attention now turns to Saturday's trip to Mainz.

#2505. Andoni Iraola has Liverpool's fearsome frontline firing, Alexis Mac Allister back to his best and is unlocking the best of Florian Wirtz... it is far too soon to count them out of the title race, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 22:00 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 08:57 EDT, 1 November 2026

Are Liverpool in the title race? The question has been bandied around this week — and conversations will only grow louder if they beat Arsenal at Anfield tomorrow.

The clash feels like an early six-pointer but regardless of the result, we can make this point — Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool are on the up and, whether this year or next, will soon be competing for the top prizes again.

This follows a season of strife in which the football was boring, the title defence fell apart and fans turned mutinous — booing, leaving early and moaning at manager Arne Slot.

The Dutchman paid with his job and in came Iraola, who — with respect to Bournemouth and Rayo Vallecano — had no experience of managing the day-to-day stresses and demands of a club of this size.

Three months into his reign, the Basque is yet to receive the plaudits he deserves. Maybe because Arsenal are champions and the two Manchester clubs are never out of the headlines, Liverpool have gone under the radar.

But they have lost just once, when down to 10 men against Manchester City, and have won their last five games, including some potential banana skins. So is it time to stop sleeping on this team’s chances?

Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool are on the up and will soon be competing for the top prizes again

Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola are starting to fire for Iraola

We can go position by position and analyse how the Reds have improved under Iraola. In attack, there was a potential narrative of a post-Mohamed Salah slump, but the absence of the Egyptian has rarely been mentioned.

In the summer, Iraola said he wants his forwards to be ‘game changers’ and he has plenty of those — Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz, Cody Gakpo and Rio Ngumoha have all fulfilled that role, plus Hugo Ekitike when he returns from injury.

In midfield, Alexis Mac Allister is back to his best and Iraola sees the Argentine as his coach on the pitch, a man who reads the game better than anyone. Wirtz is getting better while young Trey Nyoni, 19, has been outstanding when he has featured.

At the back, Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation. Fellow new signing Ronald Araujo is only on loan from Barcelona — there is an option to make that permanent — but is becoming a cult hero.

Iraola has also got the fans back on side. It is fair to say the Kop was unsure of him when he arrived but he has won them over with a front-footed, exciting style in a system that demands hard work and relentless pressing.

There is the perfect blend of youth and experience and it is clear the team are fighting for one another again.

‘It’s not just winning,’ Iraola said. ‘At Anfield, everyone feels when the team goes for it and when everyone is giving everything, trying his best… then the supporters will be there. Even when we have been losing, they have helped us massively.’

Florian Wirtz endured a difficult first season at Anfield but is starting to show why the club paid big money to sign him from Bayer Leverkusen in 2025

Jeremy Jacquet has been a revelation in the Liverpool defence

Captain Virgil van Dijk added: ‘The fans definitely like what they’re seeing and, of course, you feel that energy and it’s great. I’ve been feeling that energy for quite a while and when you miss it then to get it back is obviously very good.’

So, title race? Absolutely. Beat Arsenal and they are only three points behind the Gunners, so why not? Lose and it is nine points, which would not be insurmountable with 29 games and six months to go, but would certainly reduce the margin for error.

Usurping the Gunners might be a step too far this season, but Liverpool are certainly stronger than last term — and Iraola says there is still plenty of room for improvement.

Just look at his Bournemouth side. Winless in their first nine games, they barely looked back as they qualified for Europe. Liverpool had a rocky first month with obvious deficiencies, but are now building a head of steam.

Arsenal visit on Sunday having not won at Anfield since 2012 - last season this fixture was won by Dominik Szoboszlai's stunning 35-yard free-kick

The small details are also improving, such as solidity from set-pieces — an issue that bugged them last term with a league-high 20 goals conceded. The fitness of Isak is a huge factor, while Alisson looks in top condition again.

Asked where his team can improve, Iraola said: ‘Almost everywhere. We are defending really well lately but still we have some situations where we need to improve. In the league, we have been less dangerous offensively.

‘So it is still too early to make big conclusions but there are improvements needed everywhere.’

Arsenal might not be wary of Manchester City given potential points deductions but, should Liverpool beat them on Halloween weekend, the champions will certainly be running scared.

#2504. NWSL announces roster-building mechanisms for 2028 expansion teams

With Atlanta and Columbus joining league play in 2028, NWSL announced the return of additional allocation funds

Two expansion teams will play their inaugural National Women’s Soccer League seasons in 2028: Atlanta City FC and the to-be-named Columbus club. With the teams able to start building their rosters in 2027, the league announced Friday the mechanisms they can use to build their inaugural rosters, since they got rid of the expansion draft ahead of Boston Legacy FC and Denver Summit FC joining the league.

The options available to Atlanta and Columbus are relatively the same as the mechanisms Boston and Denver had but adjusted for the consistently increasing salary cap.

Each expansion club will have access to $1,430,000 in allocation money, roughly 30% of the 2028 base salary cap according to the announcement. Allocation money must be funded by the clubs and may be used to reduce salary cap charges, pay transfer and loan fees, and be used in trades with all other clubs. Unused, funded allocation money will remain available through December 31, 2030, including any funds subsequently traded to another club.

Comparatively, Denver and Boston had access to the same percentage of allocation money, but 50% of the funds were provided by the league and the rest funded by the teams at their discretion. They have until December 31, 2027, to use all of their funded allocation money. Allocation money purchased before 2024 via the mechanism’s original iteration will be phased out by the end of 2026, so it now appears that allocation money will live on as a unicorn available to expansion teams in the short term.

Atlanta and Columbus will also have access to an increased transfer fee threshold of $1.9 million over two years, compared to the threshold of $665,500 for non-expansion clubs in 2027. Starting on the first day of 2027 and through the conclusion of the 2028 secondary transfer window, the expansion teams have $1,167,950 available, then an additional $732,050 during the 2028 calendar year. Spending above the applicable threshold will incur a salary cap charge equal to 25 percent of the excess amount, same as the rest of the league.

For a more in-depth explanation of allocation money and transfer fee thresholds, check out this explainer from Jeff Kassouf.

In order to allow the expansion clubs to start signing players in 2027 ahead of their inaugural seasons, they will be subject to a limited salary cap of $628,320, equivalent to 14.28 percent of the 2027 base salary cap. High Impact Player (HIP) rule spending is not available until January 1, 2028.

The previous pair of expansion teams had a 6-month period during which they could sign players without being subject to the salary cap as long as they had a net-zero salary cap impact by being: loaned out to a team that picks up the full cost of salary and bonuses; qualified to be placed on SEI; or allocation money was used to cover the salary cap charge. Then they had a limited salary cap of $250,00 after the second transfer window opened.

Once again, expansion clubs will not be required to meet the league’s minimum roster size requirements in 2027 but must remain within the maximum roster size. So the players signed in 2027 can keep playing expansion clubs may loan them to clubs within or outside the NWSL. A new wrinkle for intra-league loans during 2027: the expansion clubs are permitted to retain up to 25% of the salary cap charge. Standard loan accounting rules and required roster compliance will resume in 2028.

#2503. Ashley Sanchez wins 2026 NWSL Golden Boot

20 goals ties league single-season record

North Carolina Courage attacker Ashley Sanchez has won the 2026 National Women’s Soccer League Golden Boot for scoring the most goals this regular season with a league-record-tying 20.  She also added five assists, with her 25 goal contributions ranking as the second-most in a single NWSL season.

Orlando Pride forward Barbra Banda finished close behind Sanchez with 17 goals in 23 games. Portland Thorns forward Sophia Wilson finished third with 15 goals in 28 games, including a Decision Day brace.

Sanchez started scoring early in the season with a brace in their season-opening game against Racing Louisville. She stayed on fire and ended the season with four total braces and one hat trick. Sanchez scored her 20th goal of the season, which tied the record set by Temwa Chawinga in 2024, on Sept. 27 against the Royals. However, she was unable to break the record as she was held off the scoresheet in her last three of 30 games played.

The recordings of the seminars will also be available (same price) and are included for all participants. Teaser: We will also be launching a detailed series on defending soon.

To register or to purchase the recording, just send an informal email with your name and desired date(s)/recordings to [email protected]. Payment options are PayPal and bank transfer.

Further communication will be done via mail.

Martin Rafelt is Spielverlagerung-writer and co-owner since 2011, has published a book about Jürgen Klopp, is a freelance writer for Der Spiegel, has done analysis for Thomas Tuchel and worked for three years as an assistant coach at Youth-League-finalists Hajduk Split (Under-19 and Hajduk B) and as the Head of Analysis and Tactics at the Hajduk Academy. In The 3rd Circle he discusses football philosophy.

He gave lectures at the Belgian and the Dutch FAs, works with professional players in individual analysis and as a tactical consultant for clubs. On Spox and Transfermarkt there can be found interviews.

For the first time in their history, NJ/NY Gotham FC have won the National Women’s Soccer League Shield for finishing at the top of the regular season standings.

She limped off the field under her own power and was replaced by Savannah McCaskill.

Gotham continues to add to their trophy case under head coach Juan Carlos Amoros, having won the NWSL Championship in 2023 and 2025, and now securing their first Shield.

#2500. Brosnan keeps Manchester United out as Everton earn goalless WSL draw in Crosby

To help deliver timely coverage of women's football, we may use AI tools to support content creation and editing. While we strive for accuracy and editorial quality, readers should independently verify important information.

Everton finally took something off Manchester United on Saturday 31 October, holding Eva Olid’s side to a stalemate in the FA WSL. Scott Phelan’s team had lost each of the previous 5 meetings between the clubs. At Rossett Park, goalkeeper Brosnan made sure there was no repeat, and she finished with a rating of 8.08, the highest on the pitch.

United carried slightly more of the threat. They had 9 shots to Everton’s 6, put 4 on target to their hosts’ 3 and won 5 corners to 2. Their expected goals of 0.46 doubled Everton’s 0.23, though neither figure points to a game full of clear openings.

Brosnan dealt with everything that reached her. At the other end Tullis-Joyce made 3 saves and was rated 7.41, second only to her opposite number. Possession was almost level at 49% for Everton and 51% for United.

Everton’s back line also stood out. Layzell was rated 7.15, while Blundell and Ishikawa both earned 7.11, and Blundell supplied 1 key pass as well as a shot of her own.

Referee Adewunmi Soneye showed 3 yellow cards. Van Gool was the first into the book, cautioned for a foul in the 25th minute. Simi Awujo followed for United with a foul in the 69th minute.

Andrea Medina’s booking came late. She was cautioned for dissent in the second minute of stoppage time. Everton committed 14 fouls to United’s 8, and the visitors were caught offside twice to Everton’s once.

Elisabeth Terland led the line for United in a 4-2-3-1. Everton set up in a 4-1-4-1 with Ornella Vignola as the lone forward. Neither found a way through.

Everton & Man Utd have to settle for a point each after they played out a goalless draw

United continue their unbeaten run as it’s 7 wins & 3 draws from their last 10 games

Everton have an impressive home form with only 1 loss in their last 7

— The Women’s Football Insight (@wfinsight.bsky.social) 2026-10-31T15:51:19.016Z

The point leaves Manchester United fourth on 12 points from 8 games, with a record of 3-3-2 and a goal difference of -2. They are 4 points adrift of London City Lionesses in third and 7 behind the joint leaders, Chelsea and Manchester City, who have 19 points each from 7 matches.

United are now unbeaten in 6 across all competitions, a run that includes a 1-1 draw with Manchester City, a 5-3 win over Liverpool and a 3-0 victory against Burnley last time out.

Everton are sixth with 10 points from 8 games, level with Tottenham Hotspur, who sit fifth having played once fewer. Phelan’s side came into this having beaten Sheffield United 2-1, and their recent results have alternated between wins and defeats, so a clean sheet against a side unbeaten in 5 before kick-off is a different kind of result for them.

Their next assignment is tougher still. Everton travel to Chelsea on Saturday 7 November to face the only side in the division with a perfect form line, a team that is 6-1-0 with a goal difference of 17.

#2499. The Timing Game – MH

von Next Generation am 31.03.2025 in den Kategorien Tactical Theory mit 1 Kommentar

The Timing Game describes a playing philosophy in which the right moment of an action is crucial. It not only allows pressing traps to be reversed but also enables teams to break down deep defensive blocks with precision. In the Premier League, Brighton’s then-manager Roberto De Zerbi took this tactical approach to a new level.

“Brighton is a master of passing the ball to the free man but recognising when to pass the ball to the free man and moving at the right time.” – Pep Guardiola

The core idea of the Timing Game is to react to the opponent’s movement at precisely the right moment. Pressing traps can be reversed by first triggering and manipulating the opponent’s press and then bypassing it through changes in speed and direction. Since opposition pressing actions are highly dynamic, this approach is particularly effective against high-pressing teams. Consequently, the Timing Game allows teams to dominate pressing situations in their own buildup play. Additionally, because opponent movements can be triggered independently of the game phase, the Timing Game can also be applied against deep defensive blocks.

Regarding the role of timing in De Zerbi’s buildup play, René Maric (RM) explained in a 2023 interview with SkySports:

„The biggest thing in the build-up is the control of rhythm. If you look at Guardiola, he does it with the speed of the passes and then they carry the ball when they don’t have pressure. De Zerbi does it more with the moment of the pass, the lure, the sole on the ball, opening space with the pass rather than the carry. How you control the rhythm and progress through space will be big in the future. That development has already started.“

This article examines the dimensions and functioning of the Timing Game. Additionally, it analyzes the impact of a team’s own positioning, as well as the manipulation, anticipation, and triggering of the opponent’s press (or movements). The following sections will then explore the action of bypassing the opponent, the potential issues that arise within the Timing Game, and possible solutions to these challenges.

This section is an attempt to highlight the various facets of the Timing Game and football in general. Different playing philosophies prioritize different dimensions. In the Timing Game described here, particular focus is placed on the timing of dynamics in relation to the opponent.

To gain a better understanding of the principles of the Timing Game, the following section presents and explains its different dimensions. This makes it clear how the Timing Game differs from the focus of positional play and relationism but can also be combined with them. Although the game dimensions are less important for the practical implementation of the Timing Game, they can be useful for further developing this concept or other coaching philosophies.

The most important dimension of the Timing Game is the temporal dimension. The crucial factors are the speed and timing of decision-making. The timing of a progressive action should generally coincide with the opponent’s movement. The primary focus is therefore on the exact moment of an action.

A second important dimension is that of dynamics. The dynamic dimension of the Timing Game revolves around explosiveness and changes in rhythm. Changes in dynamics can be decisive both in relation to one’s own play and in terms of directional shifts in relation to the opponent. Ultimately, the goal is to create the strongest possible reciprocal acceleration in the opponent.

In the dimension of individual performance factors, the focus is on footballing competencies such as technical and athletic abilities. In the Timing Game, ball control is a crucial factor, as it significantly affects a player’s pressing resistance. Ball control involves both the ability to recognize a situation and the technical capability to handle the ball under pressure at any time. This skill is particularly important in the Timing Game, as it provides an advantage during the opponent’s pressing phase.

The causal-relational dimension deals with the cause-and-effect principle in interactions between teammates and opponents. There is a causal relationship both between the opponent’s defensive approach and the method of bypassing them, as well as between a teammate’s action and the resulting ball action. The following examples illustrate this:

In relationism, interactions between teammates are particularly emphasized to enable optimal interplay. Due to the complexity of this dimension, I have linked MR’s seminar “The Future of the Game” here.

In the spatial dimension, the focus is on controlling specific zones of the pitch. This is particularly crucial in positional play, where the aim is to control the game through ball possession and spatial occupation. In the Timing Game, however, the goal is to reach the space behind the opponent. Since this space is constantly changing, it cannot strictly be defined as a fixed pitch zone. However, the spatial dimension does play a role in the preparatory positioning of the Timing Game. This article contains a dedicated section on the optimal positioning in preparation for the Timing Game.

In the Timing Game, the moment of an action is primarily decisive. The moment of action is always triggered by the opponent’s movement. The more intense the opponent’s movement, the easier it is to bypass them. This is because, once the Timing Game is triggered, the opponent should be bypassed as diagonally opposed to their movement as possible. This forces the opponent into a maximal change of direction and dynamics.

The pressing near one’s own penalty area is bypassed diagonally opposite to the direction of the press.

A temporal advantage is created over the opponent, who initially has to accelerate in the opposite direction and loses time. The space that opens up behind the advancing opponent can be played most effectively. Representing the functioning of the Timing Game, the principle of “Lure and Shock” could be used. The opponent is first “lured” into the movement and then “shocked” by being bypassed.

The Timing Game is particularly effective during the opponent’s transition from a deeper to a higher pressing setup. At the moment of transition between ordered pressing phases, the opponent’s structure is often lacking, as the distances between the players change. Additionally, movement is present on all positions of the opponent, which can be exploited for the Timing Game. The direction of the opponent’s movement is also crucial, as during the transition from a deeper to a higher pressing phase, vertical movement away from the goal dominates, allowing spaces towards the opponent’s goal to be exploited.

This specific moment of the opponent’s pressing transition into a higher setup cannot be found in the classic phase model of the game according to Van Gaal. Depending on the perspective, it would be classified as part of either the team’s own possession phase or the opponent’s possession phase, even though it is significantly more complex and interesting than other possession situations. The opponent is essentially in a type of defensive transition into attack from the opponent’s ball possession, while the own team takes advantage of this moment and transitions from their own ball possession into a kind of offensive transition.

The Timing Game, however, does not only work during transitions between different pressing setups, but also independently of the game phase, and thus also within the framework of the opponent’s attacking press. The opponent’s movement in attacking pressing usually does not need to be triggered additionally. Instead, it is more about anticipating the moment when the opponent’s attacking press is triggered. At the moment of pressing initiation, there is a very high dynamic on multiple positions of the opponent in (diagonal) vertical directions, which allows the pressing to be bypassed with suitable movements at the moment of initiation. Particularly, the opponent’s pressing traps can be bypassed at the moment of initiation through a corresponding pre-rehearsed anticipation and movement.

Depending on the individual pressing patterns of the opponent, preparations should be made for the timing and manner of bypassing. For example, man-marking in attacking pressing can be bypassed differently than ball-oriented or hybrid marking schemes. Particularly against man-marking, it is important in the Timing Game to initially provoke dynamics in the opponent through various runs, in order to then bypass them in the opposite direction. If dynamics are not created through own runs, there is often little movement from the opponent in the second and third layers that could be exploited.

Because dynamics are also created in the opponent’s man-marking in the second and third layers, multiple layers can be bypassed.

The pressing triggers and pressing traps also differ depending on the type of attacking press, so anticipating the moments of the Timing Game requires prior analysis of the opponent. A very commonly used pressing trigger is a backward pass to the goalkeeper from a higher defensive line. A common reaction is for the goalkeeper to play the ball long under pressure, usually resulting in a loss of possession. In the Timing Game, a team would create passing options behind the opponent through collective movements at the moment the opponent triggers their press. Specific movements and methods for bypassing the press will be discussed in more detail later in the article.

Individual pressing patterns also include the opponent’s pressing structure itself. Here too, individual weaknesses can be diagnosed and exploited in advance. When the opponent presses from a 4-4-2, they often have an under-populated central area. Of course, this cannot be generalized, as, for example, the ball-far midfielder or an aggressive center-back may situationally reinforce the center. However, if this is not the case, an inverse run by the full-back at the moment the press is triggered could be useful to play into the space behind the press against the dynamics. It can be stated that the Timing Game, against different opponents with different individual pressing patterns, influences the movements made to bypass the press.

The Timing Game can also work against deep-lying opponents. However, it is more difficult here because, in general, there is less movement away from the goal, and the opponent attacks in a more passive manner. The deep-lying opponent’s goal is to close the space near the goal. It will be crucial to trigger the opponent’s movement or pressing and lure the opponent out. We will go into more detail on such trigger actions later.

In summary, the following rules for the Timing Game depending on the opponent’s pressing can be established: The deeper the opponent is positioned, the less dynamic movement there is away from their own goal. Therefore, the time window for bypassing the press is shorter. The more passive the opponent acts, the less frequently there is opponent movement. As a result, there will be fewer opportunities to bypass the press. Nevertheless, the Timing Game can be used independently of the game phase through trigger actions.

The team’s formation in possession should be adapted to the challenges of the Timing Game. It should create central connections through a vertical/diagonal alignment. This way, more layers can be incorporated into the dynamics, and more passing options can be created. More passing windows open up at the moment of triggering through a variety of passing angles. In the event of a loss of possession, it also allows for more effective counter-pressing.

Additionally, it can be useful to work with asymmetries and overloads. Overloading the own buildup zone is particularly effective when the opponent closes down and applies high pressure. This lures the opponent and allows them to be bypassed with a few passes. In the linked video example, De Zerbi’s Shakhtar Donetsk uses a strategy of having 7 players in their own penalty area during a goal kick to lure the opponent out.

Nothing to see here, just a completely normal build-up pic.twitter.com/vOcvRPVKdf

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) April 28, 2022

Problems in the Timing Game arise when there is an overload in the own buildup zone if the opponent does not press. The progression in the game is lacking because offensive passing options are not available. Also problematic is the static overload of the last line. If players remain in their specific spaces in the last line, passing options necessary to bypass the opponent’s press are missing.

Another way to structure the team to prepare for the Timing Game is by leaving a specific area vacant. If the opponent attempts to press, this space is usually left unoccupied by the opponent as well. Subsequently, the space can be attacked and played into from the second line in the opposite direction. If the space is still occupied, the numerical advantage in a ball-near area can be exploited. Real Madrid often employs such structures or space-drawing runs in preparation for their actual attacking play with the ball.

In the Timing Game, the moment the opponent begins to press must be anticipated as early as possible. Possible indicators for early recognition of a pressing moment include: the opponent’s approach towards the ball-carrying teammate, the shrinking of distances between the ball-near opponents and their teammates, and the forward dynamics of the opponent. A defensive line with equal numbers or an advancing defender is also an early recognition feature. Lastly, specific pressing triggers should be identified through video analysis in advance.

An exemplary player for effective pressing resistance is Sergio Busquets, who, with his excellent ball control, was regularly able to anticipate and resolve pressing situations. In this 2017 article, TR and MR wrote about Busquets’ qualities.

What is particularly interesting is triggering the opponent’s attacking press. There are a variety of very interesting trigger actions. One variation used by De Zerbi is the use of the sole on the ball to wait. This plays on the impatience of the opponent. The following quote and video clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of this trigger action.

“It’s so fascinating to watch (…) when the ball goes to the center back, they freeze the game. (…) As soon as the pressing action happened, they then had this meticulously designed mechanism of up-back-throughs and third man connections (…).” – Jamie Hamilton, 3rd Circle Podcast

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) January 13, 2025

Another option is a pass triggered by speed. This pass should be played as slowly as possible and as quickly as necessary. The slow pass provokes the opponent’s pressing. At the same time, by the receiver moving towards the ball, the dynamics can immediately be reversed. This facilitates the transition into the action of bypassing or dribbling past the opponent. The pass direction should ideally be diagonal toward one’s own goal. This maximizes the reversal of dynamics.

Another approach is to play into the pressure, only to then “bounce” back into the direction of the opponent’s pressing path. The opponent is initially led to believe they have access by playing into the pressure. By bouncing the ball into the pressing direction, the opponent is forced to continue their run.

The classic way of forcing a passive opponent into movement is dribbling. The opponent is eventually made to press. However, it is also much harder to generate a dynamic shift and surprise effect, as the dribbling is already in the direction of play. Therefore, it is helpful if dribbling-skilled players attack the opponent in order to maintain the unpredictability of the next action with quick changes of direction. Alternatively, passes that bypass the opponent after dribbling in the opposite direction of the dribble path can create a dynamic shift in the opponent.

Against deep-lying opponents, the inside diagonal is a good method to force defenders on the last line to step out a few meters. When the ball is played diagonally from the outside to the center, the central defender steps out a few steps. This can be exploited in the opposite direction. The effect is enhanced by a player letting the ball pass, as immediately after, the defender’s back can be attacked. This move is known in relationism as Escadinha.

After the pressing trigger, the opponent should be bypassed through dynamic, diagonal directional changes. The direction of the first action should ideally not move away from the pressure but rather target, go over, or through it to attack the opponent’s movement. Instead of directly passing to the free player (e.g., the goalkeeper), a progressive, diagonal ball should be chosen.

To create passing options in the desired direction, specific movements are crucial. There are also various fundamental principles for this. The start of the ball action should be as late as possible but as early as necessary.

The timing of the movement of teammates should coincide with the moment the press begins, so they can be available to receive the ball under pressure, but not too early to avoid being caught by the opponent’s dynamic.

Dynamic movement should also be generated in the second and third layers to have the opportunity to bypass multiple layers. Otherwise, there is a risk of opponents from the second layer, who create covering shadows, not being affected by the opposing dynamic. In a less compact space behind the first pressing line, the dynamics can occur in stages, so the layers are played one after the other.

It is important that after an action, the next layer should be attacked immediately to maintain the dynamic.

The decisive action to overcome the opponent can be individual, group, or team tactical in nature. Below are specific examples of such actions.

A feint in the moment of pressing initiation can lead to bypassing the opponent. In the linked video, Musiala’s movement at the right moment leads to the goal. Although this movement is likely executed intuitively by Musiala at the right time, it can certainly be tactically repeated. The feint falls into the above-described phase of the pressing transition from a deeper to a higher pressing line, which is why Denmark’s player spacing is incorrect and the deep coverage is absent.

Brilliant angle of Jamal Musiala’s goal from last night. 🇩🇪#Germany #Denmark #Euro #Analysis pic.twitter.com/xl2MDgvXwb

Individually tactical, the first touch can be used both as a triggering action and as an overcoming action. By skillfully triggering the opponent’s movement, it may be enough to simply play the ball past the opponent or through their legs. The first touch is made as far as possible but as close as necessary to allow the player to regain possession of the ball immediately in front of the opponent. This is clearly seen at the very beginning of Woltemade’s first goal in the following video.

⚽#woltemade #u21 pic.twitter.com/mpdKiB4inJ

The no-look pass can also be a variant to surprise the opponent against the dynamics and running direction.

Florian Wirtz’s dribbles may initially seem unremarkable. However, upon closer observation, it becomes clear that Wirtz uses slight delays instead of flashy tricks to trigger the opponent’s movement, and then he moves the ball past the defender. This is also a form of timing play at the individual tactical level.

— thomassist (@thomassist25_) January 27, 2025

On the group tactical level, up-back-through (steil-klatsch) combinations are ideal for breaking into depth at the right moment. Here, the previously described positioning in preparation for the timing play is crucial. As many levels as possible should be occupied to open passing angles and options. The lay-off play has the advantage of being able to overcome the opponent with simple passes. It is remarkable how each of these passes is played against the opponent’s pressing direction, preventing the opponent from getting access to the ball.

— ファンキーヤング (@funkyyoung) November 19, 2024

Different variations of the play through the third man are also very effective. In the following video, the effectiveness can be admired at minute 0:13, using the example of the left center-back starting in the wrong direction.

Other possibilities in the group tactical area include one-twos against the dynamics, space-creating runs, counter movements, or dynamic zone rotations.

There are also team tactical variations for overcoming the opponent in the timing game. One such variation is playing the second ball directly into the backline with an appropriate zone overload at the moment the pressing is triggered. The preparatory positioning is the team tactical element here.

A team tactical counter movement could also be considered, where all players in the forward zones drop back, increasing the pressing distance to create more dynamic movement. At the same time, a player from the second line attacks deeply in the opposite direction.

One problem with the timing play is overcoming the covering shadow of the first pressing opponent. As the approaching opponent generates an increasingly larger covering shadow in a well-prepared pressing situation, passing options become limited. This can be solved through an individual tactical overcoming action, such as a dribble, a first touch, or others. Additionally, certain combination plays can help overcome the first pressing player. A back-up-back-through combination could be effective, where the first pass is played over a short distance to a nearby teammate (back), followed by an up-back-through combination to open new passing angles.

The short back pass to the goalkeeper, who has moved up into the defensive line, can bypass the covering shadow of the first pressing player.

Another problem could arise against teams with a very high pressing intensity. Since it is necessary to play into the pressure and trigger the pressing, one is systematically exposed to this high intensity repeatedly. However, this can also be used to one’s advantage. Opponents with high intensity also have high dynamics, which can be played against with greater effectiveness. Additionally, there is usually a high number of opponents in the attacking zones. Therefore, it is advisable to attack the farthest free space as directly as possible.

Hybrid pressing can also cause problems in the timings game. Since individual players act in specific spaces, responding situationally to regain possession of the ball, they do not necessarily carry the dynamics of the pressing players. As a result, they are more difficult to play past. However, certain off-ball runs could provide solutions here. One example would be the outside defender making a diagonal run into space far from the ball.

Lastly, there are issues when pressing the opponent during goal kicks. All playing philosophies face problems here, as the conditions to break out of the situation are not ideal. The ball is not in motion, the opponent can organize, and the playing field is limited by the goal line behind. Additionally, the risk is higher due to the proximity to the goal. The timings game would generate dynamics in the opponent by various runs from teammates, in order to reach the opponent’s back at the right moment.

The concept of dynamically timing a play to exploit the opponent’s movement at the right moment is already seen in practice. However, with a more deliberate approach, it can become more accessible to a wider range of players and even more effective. It holds the potential to bypass pressing traps and break down deep-lying defenses. It is not only applicable throughout the field but can also be effective with different numbers of players.

The dynamic timing play concept developed here is heavily focused on the reference point of the “opponent.” Another possible concept of timing could place more emphasis on the teammate, focusing on relational interactions between players. This concept would be more closely aligned with the relationalism theory. Using the dimensions outlined here, different game concepts can be created and further developed.

The timing play should be used as a complementary element to complete one’s overall playing philosophy. It provides a different perspective on tactical analysis than what would be possible with static graphics, such as those on a tactic board. Therefore, it should expand an analyst’s perspective on this complex game by adding an additional dimension.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

I know Pep Guardiola made De Zerbi the leading authority when it comes to the timing game but I also believe that Marcelino Garcia at Villarreal adds more layers to this topic. His understanding of dynamics is unique and is worth looking into.

#2498. Why you can't blame Aston Villa chiefs for fighting back at Jamie Carragher as Fulham refuse to follow pundit in backing down as they earn deserved point, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE

Published: 18:11 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 09:34 EDT, 1 November 2026

Aston Villa might have had an apology from Jamie Carragher but Unai Emery’s men found Fulham far more awkward opponents on a difficult night at Villa Park.

After Villa had threatened legal action, the Sky Sports pundit said sorry for telling ‘Aston Villa fans’ to ‘shut the f*** up’ on Saturday. The Holte End let Carragher know what they thought of him within a minute here.

Unfortunately for Villa, Fulham were in no mood to back down as Carragher had. John McGinn missed a penalty for the home side early on and though Nicolas Jackson gave them a half-time lead, Fulham deservedly equalised when Zion Suzuki – outstanding until then – carried Alex Iwobi’s corner over his own line.

Though Villa were very poor in the second half, this remains a team in transition and there will be bumps in the road. And thanks to the dispute with Carragher, the main talking point on Saturday was away from the pitch.

Villa have been mocked for this response but look at it from their point of view. The club feel that at every turn, the established order are trying to slow their progress.

Consider the financial regulations that favour historically wealthy clubs who make money off the pitch, over those who have started to succeed on it.

Nicolas Jackson has been on fire this season and netted again to give Villa the lead

Villa would certainly have settled for Champions League fixture pile-ups 10 years ago

Imagine the frustration of finishing fourth in the Premier League, winning the Europa League and then having to sell six starters from the Final.

Now he has to listen to ex-players with significant influence telling the world that Villa can never satisfy Emery’s ambition.

Carragher is probably guilty of nothing more than expressing an opinion, however crudely he may have done so. But if Sawiris is fed up of various voices and organisations trying to put Villa back in their box, who can blame him?

Whenever Antonee Robinson charged down the Fulham left, Villa were in trouble. The US international had a superb match but until his error, the visitors found Suzuki in excellent form.

He made one outstanding stop from Oscar Bobb and produced decisive interventions to deny Gonzalo Garcia, Josh King and Alex Iwobi.

There is plenty of technical ability in this side and when they move forward they are great to watch. But Garcia does not look a ruthless finisher in the style of Jackson and he missed chances here. At the back, too, they look flimsy. As well as Jackson took his goal, the challenges from Timothy Castagne and David Affengruber were weak.

Yet in Josh King and Oscar Bobb they have twinkle-toed attackers capable of threatening any defence. After a poor start to his tenure, it looks as though Alvaro Arbeloa is starting to find his range at Craven Cottage and had they won here, it would have been fully merited.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki got into a terrible mess to gift Fulham an equaliser

Villa would certainly have settled for Champions League fixture pile-ups ten years ago, when they were eking out a 1-1 draw at rivals Birmingham in the Championship, but their recent schedule has been unforgiving.

With Villa facing Barca at the Nou Camp on Tuesday, the Fulham game was brought forward from 2pm on Sunday to the late fixture on Saturday. That is exactly 72 hours after the Carabao Cup defeat to Bournemouth, and 72 before they face the Spanish champions.

Given Villa made several changes at Bournemouth, surely there was a case making this a 12.30pm kick-off, or even a 3pm kick-off on Saturday? Given the short turnaround before facing one of Europe’s strongest sides, Villa will be glad to have won their opening three games.

That gives them a clear shot at the last 16, either by qualifying directly or through the play-offs. Barcelona also opted not to rest players and fielded a strong side against Alaves in La Liga on Saturday, which was also an 8pm kick-off.

The bad news is that Hansi Flick’s side were 4-0 up at half-time and went on to win 6-1. If Fulham were able to cause Villa this much trouble with sharp passing and movement, what about the club most associated with those qualities?

Emery and his squad will certainly travel to Barcelona a little nervously on Monday afternoon.

#2497. Laimer praises Bayern's belief after Atlético win and makes bold Karl prediction

Bayern Munich secured an impressive victory in the Spanish capital on Tuesday evening, with second-half goals from Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer earning the Bavarians all three points.

Speaking to Amazon Prime after the match, Laimer was delighted with Bayern's performance, particularly given the questions surrounding the squad in recent weeks.

"We went into the game knowing what we're capable of. There has been a lot written about us and everything surrounding the team, but we have big confidence in our squad and the players we have," the Austrian said.

"I think we showed that over the full 90 minutes today: the way we can play football and the way we want to play.

"Ultimately, I think we could even have scored a few more goals. It was a thoroughly deserved win against a good team."

Laimer also reserved special praise for 18-year-old Lennart Karl, who opened the scoring in the 54th minute after winning possession inside the Atléti penalty area.

"I'm really happy for the boy. He stays calm, he wants to improve, he works hard and today he was rewarded for it.

"He showed that real fighting spirit. He tracks back, wins the ball back and then somehow manages to smash it into the net.

"He's young and still has a lot to learn. He still needs to take another step forward, but he's on a fantastic path. I'm absolutely delighted for him, and I think he has a great career ahead of him."

Laimer then discussed his stunner in the second half, which came after an excellent pass from Harry Kane, revealing that his teammates had joked about how long he took to shoot.

"The boys asked me, 'Why did you take so long to shoot?' I thought I'd take a bit more time this time before doing something too quickly, as I sometimes do, only for it not to come off properly.

"Ultimately, Harry played an outstanding pass. I controlled it, looked up to see if there was anything else I could do, and then simply finished it with a clean, composed strike.

"Sometimes you can tell as soon as the ball leaves your foot whether it's going to be a good one or not. And I immediately thought, 'Oh, yes, that feels really good!'"

After getting back to winning ways in Europe, Bayern now turn their attention to Saturday's trip to Mainz, where they will be looking to go into the international break with three points under their belt.

Chelsea beat Charlton Athletic 6-0 in the WSL on Sunday 1 November, scoring four times in the opening 19 minutes at The Oakwood in Crayford. Melvine Malard scored twice before half-time, and Bompastor’s side added two more after the break.

It took Chelsea 3 minutes to break through. Nathalie Björn finished from a Katie McCabe assist to open the scoring.

Malard made it two in the 10th minute, and Ellie Carpenter added a third in the 13th. Malard then scored her second in the 19th minute, leaving Karen Hills’ side 4-0 down long before the interval.

Malard played only 45 minutes but was rated 8.78, the highest on the pitch. Her double takes her to 4 WSL goals this season, level with team-mate James. Manchester City’s Shaw leads the scoring chart with 8.

Carpenter, rated 8.2, also created 2 chances. McCabe was busier still. Alongside her assist, she supplied 5 key passes.

Charlton’s Hutton was booked for a foul in the 50th minute, the only card of the afternoon. Seven minutes later Agnes Beever-Jones made it five, set up by Keira Walsh.

Giulia Dragoni added the sixth in the 66th minute after an assist from Alyssa Thompson.

The numbers reflected Chelsea’s control. They had 71% of the ball, completed 588 of their 665 passes and took 36 shots to Charlton’s 6. Of those, 11 were on target, against 1 from the hosts, and Chelsea’s expected goals reached 4.98 compared with 0.52.

The scoreline could have been heavier. Charlton’s goalkeeper made 6 saves and their defenders blocked 12 attempts. At the other end, Hampton was not required to make a save.

The result also follows the pattern of the clubs’ two previous meetings, both in the FA Women’s Cup. Chelsea won 4-0 on each occasion, at Charlton in January 2020 and at home on 12 January 2025.

To help deliver timely coverage of women's football, we may use AI tools to support content creation and editing. While we strive for accuracy and editorial quality, readers should independently verify important information.

Granadilla Tenerife beat Athletic Club 2-0 in Liga F on Monday 2 November, with Padilla and Gramaglia scoring after a goalless first half in Santa Cruz de Tenerife. Athletic had gone four league matches without defeat before the trip to the island.

Neither side found a way through before half-time. The only incident of note came in the 42nd minute, when Quiles was booked for a foul.

The deadlock lasted until the 51st minute. Zaremba provided the assist and Padilla finished to put the hosts ahead.

Athletic picked up two bookings as they chased the game. Martínez was shown a yellow card in the 53rd minute and Valero followed her into the referee’s notebook in the 73rd. Granadilla’s Muina Asla was cautioned in the 79th minute, leaving the card count level at two apiece for referee Calvo.

Gramaglia settled it in the 89th minute. Her goal doubled the lead and sealed a clean sheet for the home side.

This was another strong evening for Granadilla in this fixture. Athletic have now failed to score in the last three meetings: a 0-0 draw in August 2025, a 5-0 defeat on the island in January 2026 and this result. Granadilla have also won their last three home games against the Basque side, going back to a 2-1 victory on 2 November 2024.

The win continues a productive run for the hosts, who have taken four victories from their last five matches. Their only defeat in that stretch was a 3-2 loss to Real Madrid.

After nine rounds, Athletic are fifth on 15 points with a record of four wins, three draws and two defeats. Granadilla are sixth on 14 points, and their goal difference now stands at zero.

Both sides sit within touching distance of the places above. Atlético Madrid are fourth on 16 points and Madrid CFF third on 17, while Barcelona lead on 24 ahead of Real Madrid on 22.

Athletic face the harder assignment next. They host second-placed Real Madrid on Saturday 7 November. Granadilla are at home again on Sunday 8 November, when 14th-placed Deportivo Alavés, who have 8 points from nine games, visit.
