#2435. Aspect analysis: Leipzig never found a trigger – LC

von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren

A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart. Look at how the goals came about one by one and a different picture emerges: it was not six separate problems but two or three, which Bayern punished in seven variations. No pressure on the man in possession, marking problems in central areas, and a back line that did not work with the movements in front of it – that chain runs through practically every goal conceded.

This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.

Bayern triggered very high throughout, stayed tight to their opponents and pushed through centrally without hesitation. Vandevoordt was pressed from Bayern’s right, with the clear intention of keeping him away from the left-hand build-up route and forcing the long ball. Leipzig’s front line of Nusa and Brajan Gruda repeatedly angled their runs deep against Nathaniel Brown and Konrad Laimer.

Bayern had one extra central player dropping into midfield in this phase, usually Kimmich. Had Leipzig played short to the right, he could have pressed through onto Raum; in practice he stayed central and pushed through from there. That left Leipzig with the long ball, and it was ineffective: it produced almost no regains, so the enforced forward play brought neither relief nor territory.

Going the other way, Leipzig got no access at all, and the reason was Bayern’s rotations. Kimmich dropped right, Pavlović left into a back three, with Upamecano holding a very wide position. Against this shifting three-man build-up Leipzig never found a trigger, because the assignments reset with every rotation – whoever was supposed to step out of midfield first had to work out who he was picking up. The handover of pressing duties out of central areas failed repeatedly.

In front of that, Bayern staggered their shape so that Leipzig’s compactness became the problem. Olise moved into the ten space at times, Nathaniel Brown operated in the half-lane and ran beyond from there, Luis Díaz stayed wide left. Saibari and Kane pinned several opponents centrally while regularly pulling out of the central lane. Because Leipzig pressed very narrow, this produced exactly what Bayern were looking for: once the opponent was committed near the ball, the switch followed, and on the now open side stood a one-on-one.

That already builds the bridge to the goals. The isolated one-on-ones in which Luis Díaz got his three finishes were not individual moments but the product of this sequence of pinning and switching.

1-0, Luis Díaz (12.) – The first goal already contains the full diagnosis. Kimmich receives centrally without any pressure and can turn out with an open body shape. Ahead of him Saibari and Kane occupy the central zone in front of the box, which forces Orban and Lukeba to step out – so far, the intended part. The full-backs, however, do not push up with that movement and stay too deep, while Raum’s position plays the runner onside. Klostermann stays outside and leaves the inside lane unsecured, and that is exactly where Luis Díaz starts from. Out of that unprotected lane Díaz runs into the back line and Kimmich chips the ball in behind. Not one bad decision, but four players whose decisions did not fit together.

2-0, Aleksandar Pavlović (26.) – Same cause, different route. Kane drops deep and Leipzig do not shift across as a unit – the reactions showed it clearly: arms thrown up, gesturing, hands dropping again, the beginnings of frustration. Kane gets the free body shape, and with him the consequence is predictable: the long ball, high or flat. Because Leipzig are so narrow centrally, the ball flies straight through the entire zone in front of their back line. Luis Díaz moves actively into the passing lane to control it while Klostermann tries to get into his running line and does not make it – Díaz reaches the ball first. From the one-on-one he wins, Díaz dribbles centrally at Orban, which creates a four-against-three on the break. Díaz pins Orban and Lukeba centrally, Pavlović overlaps on the left after holding a high, left-leaning position all evening and threatening the back line. Two touches, left foot, finished away from the defender.

3-0, Michael Olise (34.) – Here Bayern’s press shows itself at its clearest. From a Leipzig throw-in, the man-orientation is fully visible: consistent pushing through, clean handovers. A misplaced pass from Raum then cannot be defended, because neither the tracking nor the duelling is good enough to disturb the pass. Kane can open up half-way. Centrally, Olise comes inside from the wing, and Banzuzi and his partner fail to pick him up, letting him run through – against a player of that variability, an invitation to the key pass. Luis Díaz runs beyond and drags Orban with him, Klostermann is pinned wide by Saibari and can no longer get back into central areas. Olise finishes against the goalkeeper’s movement, across his standing leg into the far corner, catching Vandevoordt completely on the wrong foot.

4-0, Luis Díaz (47.) – After a regain, Bayern switch quickly to the far side and once diagonally through, putting Díaz in a one-on-one again. He holds the ball in the dribble, and Leipzig fail to solve the situation in three steps: the centre is not closed, Orban is too late stepping out, Klostermann does not get into the duel. That Vandevoordt leaves the far corner open is the final piece of an isolated one-on-one that should never have arisen.

5-0, Harry Kane (53.) – Structurally the most interesting goal. Leipzig play a long ball without preparing it and react to the consequences contradictorily: the back line does not push up at all, while the midfield line and both forwards counterpress forwards. The ten space opens up enormously, the gaps between the lines become huge – and Olise is standing in that zone. One pass from Kim is enough to take six Leipzig players out of the game. Olise runs unopposed at the back line and lays it off to Díaz, who is in a one-on-one again; Brown joins for the two-against-one and shifts into the inside lane. Klostermann does not pick up his run from the deep half-space, and centrally Kane again drops into Orban’s blind side – a pattern that stood out across the whole game. The result is a two-against-one against the goalkeeper.

6-0, Luis Díaz (69.) – From a set piece Bayern create a five-against-four out wide. Gnabry pins opponents and makes the space for Díaz, Orban again takes one big step in the block and does not get into the duel. The same scene as the 4-0, only from a different phase of play – a sign that this is a behavioural pattern rather than a snapshot.

6-1, Andrija Maksimović (90.+1) – Leipzig’s goal shows in reverse what their own game had been missing. Bayern drop into a deeper block here, and Leipzig combine centrally before going wide. Gruda gets into a one-on-one against Brown, Upamecano steps across – but from above, with too wide a gap and without closing the centre. That opens the one-two, which Leipzig take immediately. Because the whole situation narrows onto that combination, the space behind it stays unoccupied, and Maksimović can take two touches on his left and finish unopposed.

The sequence of goals reads like a repetition. Five of Bayern’s six come from the same combination of no pressure on the ball centrally and a back line that does not manage the space behind it. Luis Díaz stands in an isolated one-on-one three times, Orban is twice too late with a step that is too big, Kane repeatedly drops into his blind side. Klostermann certainly did not have his best day – but it would be too easy to settle the bill with him. In the decisive scenes he faced situations that functioning protection in front of him should never have allowed to arise in the first place.

Behind it all lies not an individual problem but a structural one: Leipzig pressed narrow and found no trigger against Bayern’s rotating back three. That very compactness made the switch of play the opponent’s most effective tool, and at the end of every switch stood a one-on-one that Leipzig lost. The scoreline is not the story – the story is that the same scene worked six times.

LC is often found in a classroom, happiest on a football pitch, and occasionally on LinkedIn.

#2434. Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin desperate to end his trophy drought by lifting the Premier Sports Cup

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 14:23 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:23 EDT, 1 November 2026

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin insists he is desperate to finally end his own personal trophy drought after reaching the Premier Sports Cup final.

Raskin has been at Rangers for almost four years but is yet to actually lift any silverware, something which he does not seek to shy away from.

The Belgian midfielder missed the final of this competition in December 2023 due to injury as Rangers beat Aberdeen 1-0 – and therefore did not collect a winner’s medal.

After beating the Dons by the same scoreline at Hampden last night, Rangers are now through to next month’s final against Hibs as they aim to secure the first trophy of the season.

Raskin freely admits that the fact his trophy cabinet is still bare after almost four years is something which annoys him. But it is something he is determined to rectify.

‘I just want to go and win it,’ said the 25-year-old. ‘My family tell me I’ve won one (trophy), but I tell them I haven’t.

Rangers star Nico Raskin wants to make up for missing the 2023 Premier Sports Cup final

Manager Derek McInnes joins Raskin and his Rangers team-mates after their semi-final victory

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi celebrates scoring the winner against Aberdeen at Hampden

‘When we won this competition previously, I got rested for the first two games - and injured for the next two.

‘So that’s not me winning it. Yeah (it annoys me). I think I’ve been here a long time and we’ve worked so hard.

‘Not having that is difficult, but hopefully next month we’ll win one. I’m just happy to get to this final with full belief and I want to win that cup.

‘It’s top. It’s really good for the team. But now we want to win it and there’s one game to go. Now we go full force to win the cup.’

After almost leaving Rangers at various points over the past year, Raskin insists he is now fully focused on delivering success over the rest of this campaign.

He was made captain yesterday by Derek McInnes and was glad to repay the manager’s faith with a hard-fought victory.

Despite toiling to break down a stubborn Aberdeen side, Rangers finally broke through when Ryan Naderi stabbed home from close range with only seven minutes remaining.

If Rangers can go on and lift the cup in next month’s final, Raskin believes it could pave the way for further success this season.

‘Listen, it’s not going to be an easy season. It’s a long season,’ he said. ‘But the main thing is to keep focused and keep working towards the goal.

‘We need to keep believing in the manager and what we’re doing, then we’ll be there.

‘Things happen for a reason (in terms of what happened with transfer interest) and I’m looking forward to that game next month in the final.

‘Hopefully we can achieve something good this season that will lead us to a more exciting season.

‘Aberdeen gave us a difficult game. If you think you’re going to have an easy game, coming out and winning 4-0, you’re wrong.

‘The other team is coming with a plan and it’s a big game for them, also. It’s not easy to win football games. So you go out and give the best performance you can.

‘We won, so we’re very happy. In terms of the manager, he breathes Rangers and he gives that to us.

‘It’s so good to have someone like him driving us every day and on the pitch. I’m delighted for him and hopefully we can win it for him too.

‘He told us that it wasn’t going to be easy. That if we turn up and do everything we have to do, then we’d win the game.

‘We couldn’t come out with complacency and think it would be easy to score four goals. It’s a hard game that isn’t easy to win, so we have to enjoy it when we do.’

#2432. Access, Not Chances: How Como Took Manchester United Apart – LC

von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren

Como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game. For long stretches the match was one-sided, not in terms of chance volume but in terms of access: Como dictated in every phase where the ball went, who received it, and under what conditions it had to be played on. United never got on terms in any of those phases.

Cesc Fàbregas’s side showed two things that rarely go together. Out of possession, a pressing structure with clear direction, isolation of one side, and man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress while everything around it was already speculating on the second ball. And in possession, a positional game of remarkable technical maturity that ties opponents in, switches play, and works systematically into the space behind them. The 4-1 is therefore less an outlier than evidence of work that has been built up over recent seasons.

This analysis goes through the phases one by one: first Como in possession and United’s response, then the work against the ball from the high press to defending the box, and finally the goals.

In build-up, Como moved away from their nominal 4-2-3-1 and sat closer to a 4-3-3, with the eights as the real variable: very free in their movement and above all active in the half-spaces. The base structure stayed stable — a flat four plus a six in front of them, sometimes ahead of the line, sometimes slightly behind the forward line.

Close to their own goal, Como consistently involved goalkeeper Butez as an additional central player in the build-up. That created a five-against-four against United’s front line — awkward on paper, more awkward still in execution, because Como didn’t use the overload to play through but to tie opponents in. From there, the same shape kept appearing on both the right and the left: centre-back, full-back, a player from the half-position in the eight space, and a six alongside. A diamond that wasn’t an end in itself but had a purpose: the diagonal route out.

Como’s build-up structure. From a 4-1 (flat four), the half-positions with Paz and Perrone are added. Small triangles and diamonds emerge. The three attackers ahead of them create additional options in behind.

One detail deserves particular attention. At times the full-backs stood not wide but flat, in a half-position. That sounds like a nuance, but it had a clear function: it vacated the wing and created the space the eights could drop into — Paz and Perrone did so regularly. If you don’t occupy the wing yourself, you force the opponent to guard it anyway.

ManU got no access near the ball and left large diagonal spaces open on the far side.

For United’s midfielders this was close to unsolvable. Tielemans, Mount and Andrey Santos spent the whole game struggling to establish any responsibility at all, let alone get into duels. When an eight dropped out, they couldn’t follow, and if one of them was tied in by it, a two-against-one opened up on the far wing. Como didn’t create that situation once; they created it serially.

The decisive mechanism lay in receiving and relaying the ball. The player in the deeper position usually worked with two touches: the first took the ball backwards, the second relayed it to the free teammate. At the end of every one of those actions stood a player with the game in front of him — and from that open position he could switch play.

What made it possible were the preparatory movements. Paz and captain Da Cunha first lured their markers in the wrong direction and then worked with the head start they’d bought. That head start isn’t only space, it’s above all time: time to control the ball first and relay it second, rather than having to do both in one touch.

A scene in the 17th minute is typical. Mason Mount steps out, Mazraoui goes into the duel at the same time — nominally United are in an overload here. Only neither of them really gets to the opponent, because both are too late. Paz can therefore calmly take his touch backwards and switch play directly with the second, dissolving the pressure before it had even formed.

When the build-up ran down the right, it showed in a recurring pattern: Paz and Da Cunha took the first touch backwards or inside and then switched with the left foot out of a closed body position. The players they found were systematically in open positions — Milla, the far-side six, or the wing-to-wing connection directly.

In the second half, Como adjusted the shape and more often played with two sixes, to form the diamonds faster and switch to the far-side six faster. Couto stood out in this: the right-back repeatedly played the chip into the six or ten space — six or seven times in a row during one spell. It was mainly Paz who received the ball there and could launch the attack.

In the second half Como focus on those diagonal spaces and look for them mainly with chipped balls.

Especially striking inside the diamond are the rotations between the players. Because of the connections between them, they moved in rotation depending on running path, space and ball movement. The same recurring spaces were re-occupied. Under pressure on the ball carrier, the outer players pushed flat or ran in behind the opponents; the highest player in the diamond burst out of the cover shadow and became the reference point in depth. On a deep pass, the two wide players released and joined the depth, able to offer themselves again immediately in an open body position. If the pass went via the flat wide players, the spaces in front of the new ball carrier could be run into. Every rotation, every positional adjustment was coordinated with the others and, in the end, produced a stream of pressure-resolving passes while Manchester United chased the press in vain.

Como bridged the middle third exceptionally quickly, via dribbles at speed and diagonal passes. Behind it stood a recognisable principle: first tie the opponent to one wing, then get behind them via the diagonal, and in the final third do the same thing again. In sum, that produced the shape of a Z — build-up on the right, transition on the left, finish from the right again.

In this example Como pin ManU in the press with their short passing. Thanks to the extra attacker on the ball-near side they can play through the pressure and switch.

The connections between wingers and striker carried these attacks and were deliberately kept flexible. The wide players sometimes stayed wide, sometimes came short, sometimes tucked inside. Douvikas accordingly either waited deep in front of the line for the chipped ball or, when space opened up on the wing, received the deeper pass and then ran in behind along the wing as soon as the ball sat on the full-back’s open foot. That flexibility produced the overloads on one side, and the overloads produced the central overload.

In the final third one element was added that is rare in fast transition teams: patience. Como drew opponents towards them with dribbles and short passes, used back-passes when needed, and then switched in front of the block. Da Cunha, Baturina and Paz were the three who could tie opponents in and then find the diagonal. They created the positions on the diagonal, were available to receive, and used their space to apply pressure. The block was usually tied in with short touches, the switch and the position behind the opponent prepared, and quick finishes sought.

The intensity in possession shouldn’t be underestimated. Practically every attack involved at least three or four players, the width was occupied, the centre likewise, and there were multiple options throughout. What they looked for almost every time was the space behind the opponent on the far side — exactly the zone that is closed last when a block shifts across.

Paz brought the right profile for this pattern. A strong left foot cutting inside from the right, he repeatedly dropped into the right-hand blind side of his opponents, got shots away there with few touches, and racked up the most shots of the match. That the finishes generally came off few touches isn’t a detail but the consequence of the time won further back.

As the move continues, Como again look for the blind side of the defenders. Here Douvikas and Paz are positioned in behind, with Da Cunha joining in front of the back line. After briefly pinning the opponents, the switch reaches Da Cunha, who misses the target from distance.

What carries all of this is the technical execution. Soft passes, sharp ones when the moment called for it, consistently well timed and played into the right foot — for ninety minutes. Passing that secure at that tempo is what makes a variable concept actually retrievable.

United’s basic problem out of possession was the hybrid. They pressed half man-oriented, but with a plus-one in the last line — a construction that forces compromises in both directions. It demands access up front that it doesn’t fund at the back.

There were certainly moments when it worked. When Dalot pushed through into the press on the right and passed his man backwards, a clean man-orientation emerged all the way up to the front — and with it a clear assignment for Mount, out of which the ball could be won. But that stayed the exception. Most of the time Dalot sat too flat out of possession, so United couldn’t trigger the duels up front and went into the press a man short.

Mount was the most conspicuous case in this respect. He barely got into a duel across the whole match because the decision to step out always came too late. Against a team that works with preparatory movements, a late decision is practically the same as none: the opponent already has the head start before the journey even begins.

On top of that came a problem on the far side. There, United’s winger frequently failed to protect the depth — usually Mbeumo, who jogged back rather than closing the space. But that was precisely the target zone of Como’s diagonal switches. It allowed them to change sides almost at will and regularly find an open structure on the other side.

The second half brought no improvement. The distances to opponents stayed large, and centrally what was actually intended still didn’t materialise. Michael Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring more physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it didn’t solve the problem — the assignments still didn’t work, the duels in the centre still didn’t happen, and the wide positions dragged the eights out further, which opened new spaces.

In the end the energy simply wasn’t there to press with the necessary intensity. United’s press became increasingly static, and a static press against an opponent with this passing quality yields not a single ball win — it only hands them the starting positions they’re looking for anyway.

Como started the game in a high press and sustained it above all in the first half, with isolated spells after the break too. It was triggered on back-passes and goal kicks — and, remarkably, by their own goals: after every strike the team immediately pushed high again instead of managing the lead in a deeper block.

The steering ran consistently towards United’s left build-up side. The reason is personnel: Harry Maguire played there with his weaker left foot as the outside foot, and next to him stood another right-footer in Noussair Mazraoui on the left. Two right-footers on one build-up side means the ball always has to be taken back inside to play on — exactly where Como were closing the door. The press was usually triggered by the left-sided forward, with the ball ending up at either Maguire or Mazraoui.

Pressing structure after the change in the second half.

In the centre Como defended man-oriented, with both sixes pushing very high and taking flat passes into United’s midfielders out of the game. That removed the short route through the middle as an option and left the long ball. But the long ball triggered nothing for United: the second balls went to Como practically every time.

That isn’t chance, it’s running work. The sixes consistently tracked the negative pressing paths back, anticipated the long ball early, and were in front of the line before it arrived. Luis Milla covered the most ground of any player on the pitch in this pattern — recovery runs after being played past, doubling up on the ball, attacking the second ball. When the long ball came from Maguire or one of the full-backs, a six was regularly in front of the line with an intense sprint, sealing the centre, taking away the diagonal follow-up passes and attacking the loose balls.

Defending the long ball and extra support on the second ball.

Once the ball was on one side, that side was isolated. The near-side forward had access to the centre-back and dropped back a touch when the pass went to the full-back, so that he covered centre-back and six simultaneously and closed the square pass. The far-side forward marked the goalkeeper. That served two functions at once: it took away United’s escape route via the keeper along with the switch, and it kept a player in position for the moment of the turnover.

The double pivot worked in a deliberate half-position. The near-side six stayed tight to his man, the far-side one dropped slightly behind him — securing the space and at the same time establishing access to the far-side centre-back in United’s back three.

The last line defended largely man-for-man in the high press, and very tightly. But the decisive detail is the one that carries the whole concept: the man-marking near the ball applied only to the action in progress. Around it, players were already releasing from their assignments and orienting towards the second ball. That is only retrievable at very high intensity — and it’s the reason United’s forced long balls produced not a single usable moment.

When Como dropped a line, the man-orientation at the second height stayed exceptionally high. Here too the back-pass served as the trigger to push up as a unit and tip back into man-marking. If United were in a closed body position, the Comaschi had already pushed up far enough to attack the back-pass at the moment it was played — a pattern that led directly to the 3-0. The half-position was at work there again: closing down level with the centre-back while simultaneously prepared to push through onto the next player deeper.

In the first half Como still had problems assigning the half-positions against ManU’s 3-2-5. In this example Fernandes moves to the wing, Como fail to establish responsibility and access and are played through at mid-height.

Up to half-time, though, Como had a structural problem with this. The pure man-marking didn’t come off cleanly, because of the two sixes in front of the line, one should really have tucked in and taken over the half-position for the centre-backs. That didn’t happen consistently. The consequence: a centre-back stepped out, the space behind him stayed unoccupied, and that was exactly what United kept attacking.

The pattern of pressing onto Manchester United’s left side continued in the second half, now with Dalot at full-back. The press was still triggered by Douvikas, with the ball-near winger pushing up as a second striker to press the centre-back. Paz focused on the visitors’ ball-near six and Couto pushed through onto Dalot. Through the central connections the game was isolated on one side.

At half-time Como adjusted. One six moved directly into the line, with the far-side winger pushing in onto the six — they now pressed out of a 5-2-1-2. Lucas Da Cunha pressed through from the right onto Maguire, while Nico Paz picked up United’s six. The central forward pressed the central centre-back and from there carried on to the goalkeeper. The far-side wide midfielder and the remaining six were poised — one onto United’s free six, one onto the far-side centre-back — again in that half-position between opponent and the space to be protected.

ManU building up high against the man-oriented Italians.

The effect was immediately visible. Como controlled the half-positions, got access right into the last line throughout, and set the rhythm of the match from then on. The adjustment solved exactly the problem the first half had left open, without changing the underlying principle.

In the final phase Como defended from a very deep line inside the box. That left barely any space behind the line to play into — which United hardly looked for anyway. The visitors attacked little depth and rarely occupied the width in the final third, so Como could stay compact without being punished for it.

Accordingly, a lot of players stood very centrally in and in front of the box. That produced numerous cover shadows and a numerical superiority around the ball, which allowed them to steer actively within the block rather than merely react. At times they deliberately steered inside, to guide the opponent into the prepared congestion and cover from a deeper position.

Deep back line in the box, centre closed and play steered inside. The box defending allowed the English side shots from distance.

The crucial point is that Como left the gaps open not despite this set-up but because of it. If you pack the box and secure the depth, you give up the space in front of the line — and that is exactly where United were supposed to shoot from.

The numbers vindicate the decision. Taking the conceded goal out of the box, Como allowed nine shots from outside the penalty area across ninety minutes, worth roughly 0.24 xG combined; only three of them were even on target. On top of that, of the four shots inside the box, two came from at least 14 to 15 metres and effectively belong in the long-range category as well. United accepted the invitation, and the shooting quality was perfectly decent — it’s just that with that scoring probability over a whole match, the most likely outcome is precisely what happened.

1-0, Nico Paz (2′) — The goal comes before United are even set. Como take the goal kick quickly and play straight to the full-back, luring the visitors into the press — only not cleanly. Mason Mount triggers the pressure and is played past, and on the second ball he goes into the duel as well instead of holding the middle and looking for the space where he could pick the ball up. That is exactly what opens the centre, the space for the second ball is there, and Paz can play it through.

What follows is the transition principle in its purest form: a quick switch to the diagonal side, then short passes against a very deep line. Matheus Cunha doesn’t pick up the player behind him and leaves the ten space open, where Paz is standing. He needs two touches because neither Cunha from above nor Maguire from his distance gets into the duel. Lammens, for his part, doesn’t defend the goal with his cover shadow but takes the near post — which leaves the far corner to a strong left foot. The curled finish into it is quality, though.

2-0, Anastasios Douvikas (49′, assist Paz) — Same zone, same cause. Bryan Mbeumo doesn’t choose to shut the centre but closes the centre-back, which creates the space for Da Cunha, who drives forward and plays Martin Baturina in. Centrally, Mount again fails to pick up his man. Out wide, Amad Diallo, introduced at half-time, generates no pressure centrally, so Mazraoui can’t take over the deep wide player in the first place.

The result is Paz behind the opponent, in the ten space, dribbling unopposed at goal. Matthijs de Ligt establishes no reference to Douvikas’s run in behind and slips as well — a one-against-one with the goalkeeper that Douvikas finishes coolly.

3-0, Nico Paz (57′) — The only goal that comes directly out of the work against the ball. Como are in the midfield press in a closed position with access to the inside lane, win the ball there and punish a lapse of concentration in the visitors’ build-up. At the end, Paz is alone in front of Lammens again.

4-0, Jacobo Ramón (76′, assist Kaiki) — This goal comes from a longer possession spell and shows the assignment problem in its clearest form. Mazraoui is too narrow and has no access to the wide player. Diallo stands in the space with access to neither the central player nor the full-back nor the winger — an orientation that doesn’t work in any direction.

Como switch to Máximo Perrone, who can slide the ball out wide because the space is simply free. From there comes the cross from an open body position, and in the centre Como run a two-against-one at the end of which Ramón scores.

4-1, Joshua Zirkzee (90′) — Como’s only lapse, and one in a phase in which the team had already dropped very deep. United get the ball to the wing, it’s two against two in the box, and the cross is initially only feinted. Zirkzee orients himself well forwards at that moment, while Como’s defenders are already stepping out after the feinted cross. Diallo’s ball in behind the line is strong, the offside call is razor-thin in his favour, and Zirkzee takes two touches before finishing one-against-one with the goalkeeper. A blemish, not a structural problem.

The common denominator — Three of Como’s four goals come in the same zone: the space in front of and behind United’s line that nobody takes responsibility for. Mount is involved in two of those scenes through an assignment he never establishes, Diallo in two more after coming on. Nico Paz is at the heart of three of the four goals, twice as scorer, once as the provider — always out of the opponent’s blind side.

Como’s 4-1 has one common cause across every phase, and it lies less in any single idea than in its execution under continuous load. Out of possession they steered, isolated and speculated on the second ball — with man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress and was already dissolved around it. In possession they tied opponents in, switched play and worked systematically into the space behind. Both require eleven players to anticipate a teammate’s decision, and both functioned over the full distance.

The connecting detail is the half-position. In the press, the far-side six stood between opponent and the space to be protected; in possession, the eights worked out of the same zone, and the full-backs occupied it flat in order to vacate the wing for exactly those players. Como, in other words, occupied the position in both directions from which two jobs can be done at once — which is why the side could neither be played past in the press nor be pinned in the build-up.

For United the diagnosis is more uncomfortable than the result. The problem wasn’t individual errors but that the team never, in any phase, got into the duels it needed. The mixture of half man-orientation and a plus-one in the last line funded no access up front, and without access every decision is made too late — from Mount in the centre to Mbeumo failing to secure the far-side depth. Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it changed nothing about the assignments, and in Diallo a player came on wide who reached neither one opponent nor the other in his space. That the energy ran out in the end was a consequence rather than a cause.

That leaves the context. A 4-1 against Manchester United is no proof in itself, and Como’s finishing was exceptionally efficient on the night. What showed regardless of the result, though, is a team with a recognisable, rehearsed answer in all four phases of the game — and one that put a technical maturity on the pitch in possession that you wouldn’t readily credit to a side promoted two years ago.

#2431. Hearts 1 Hibs 2: Reedijk's first victory is one to remember as spirited Leith men battle back to see off rivals and reach Premier Sports Cup final

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:25 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:33 EDT, 1 November 2026

If you are going to keep your supporters waiting until your fifth match in charge to record your first victory, best to make it a good one.

For Marink Reedijk and the Hibs fans, this pulsating triumph over their great rivals proved to be a classic case of better late than never.

By the end of a remarkable weekend, the fact the Easter Road side had dropped to the foot of the Premiership table wasn’t even so much as a mild concern.

Hibernian will return to Hampden in December 13 to face off against Rangers for the first major trophy of the season.

Just as significantly, they got there with a performance which was brave and brilliant.

After a difficult start to life in Leith, Reedijk belatedly announced his arrival with a storied victory.

McGrath fires home a rebound to put Hibs in front just before half time

Reedijk embraces goalscorer Boyle as he is substituted in the second half

Whatever happens next month against Derek McInnes’ side, Hibs have created history just by getting this far.

Their four previous jousts with Hearts at Hampden stretching back to 2006 had all ended in failure.

How those witnesses to those disappointments milked the moment at time up here as Sunshine on Leith echoed around the arena.

Reedjik’s men did not make life easy for themselves. They were behind inside four minutes when Claudio Braga struck.

Given how poor their league form has been of late, you wondered if it might get ugly. What did we know?

Hibs were scintillating until the interval, on the front foot and turning the game on its head through Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

While they defended like their lives depended on it when Hearts came at them in the second half, they spurned chances to put the game to bed.

Not that they’ll care a jot about that now. Under Reedijk, they finally have lift-off.

This was a painful episode for Wouter Vrancken, the Hearts manager.

It was as if the dream start startled his players. They were never in control of the contest the minute Hibs dusted themselves down and got to work.

Braga faded from view and he was not the only one. There was an air of desperation to Hearts’ efforts long before referee David Dickinson put them out of their misery.

The truth is that all the best players on the day - Joe Newell, Owen Elding and Boyle chief among them - wore the green of Hibernian.

Accordingly, Hearts’ wait for a first League Cup since 1962 goes on.

The bookmakers had predicted a win for the Tynecastle side. The form book pointed towards it. And, after just four minutes, so did the scoreline.

Calvin Miller won and took a corner at the Hibs end which swung in viciously. Braga timed his run to perfection, ghosted into space and planted a header beyond Raphael Sallinger.

Braga gets free at a corner to head Hearts into an early lead at Hampden

After two own goals in his past two matches, Jason Kerr could have lived without the finger of blame pointing towards him.

On the sidelines, Reedijk looked on impassively. How would his side respond? In the best way imaginable, as it happened.

Rather than going into their shells, Hibs went on the attack and completely dictated the minutes up until the half-time whistle. To a man, they were simply outstanding.

Newell was at the heart of everything, demanding the ball in tight areas, finding passing angles which no one else could.

He played a cute pass to Felix Passlack. Goal-side of Malachi Fagan-Walcott, he forced Beau Reus into a low save.

Hearts’ cause certainly wasn’t helped by a couple of early withdrawals through injury.

Tomas Magnusson never recovered from a head knock he sustained in a clash with Kerr. Yan Dhanda shed his tracksuit.

Miller tried to run off a muscular injury that required treatment but was eventually replaced by Sabri Guendouz.

But there was more to the change in the game’s flow than just the personnel.

Hibs were far more secure in possession. They were more inventive. They looked more dangerous.

Adam Mayor’s pace took him to the line. His cut-back ended with Elding blazing over. But it encouraged the men in green and white.

Their equaliser on 19 minutes came after a period of control.

Newell’s pass into Elding was played with the perfect pace and direction. Elding’s flick around the corner was precise.

Running off Fagan-Walcott’s shoulder, Boyle got enough on his shot to prevent Reus’ touch keeping it out of the net.

Boyle squeezes his shot through Hearts goalkeeper Reus to bring Hibs level

Any concern among the Hibs fans that their celebrations would be cut short by VAR were ended when a still image showed Jordi Altena playing Boyle on by a couple of inches.

Hibs’ determination to stay on top extended to deserved bookings for Kerr and Josh Mulligan for taking out Dhanda and Stephen Kingsley. Altena was also carded for clipping Boyle.

Newell clipped the top of the crossbar with a drive through a packed penalty box.

Three minutes from the break, Newell was instrumental in the move which saw his side deservedly go up the tunnel ahead.

Boyle’s corner was headed clear by Jamie McCart. Newell took a brilliant touch to take Braga out of the game. His fizzing shot was blocked on the line by Fagan-Walcott. McGrath kept his nerve from four yards to stab the ball home.

Hearts had started well but completely dropped their levels. Braga did flash a header from a Josh McPake cross narrowly wide in injury time but an equaliser was ill-deserved at that point.

You sensed Vrancken would go through his players in the dressing room.

They were better after the turnaround. Laurent Mendy curled a shout just over while Braga raced clear and forced Sallinger to make a solid stop at his near post.

While Boyle did dart in from the left and force Reus to save, Hearts were asking more of the questions.

When Reedijk’s men came up for air, Elding’s hopes of nicking a third were thwarted by McCart’s slide tackle. Kerr also headed straight at Reus.

Sallinger did well to prevent Guendouz’s net-bound strike creeping in under his bar.

The Easter Road side take the acclaim of supporters after booking their spot in the final

With the game increasingly stretched, Kingsley made up the ground to deny Passlack.

What Hibs fans would have given for a third to seal the deal.

Thibault Klidje should have done so when he burst clear with seven minutes remaining. With better options to his right, he took the wrong one and fired harmlessly over. At least he worked the keeper with his next attempt.

Hibs battened down the hatches. Grant Hanley came on and, this week, there was no debate about what end of the field he’d be stationed.

When Braga headed a chance from a free-kick wide with a couple of minutes remaining, the maroon exodus began.

Wild horses couldn’t have dragged the Hibs supporters from the arena. How they savoured this.

#2430. PSG and Premier League clubs eyeing El Mala as Köln raise asking price

After being linked with a host of clubs during the summer transfer window, Said El Mala ultimately stayed at 1. FC Köln, signing a contract extension until 2031.

However, this doesn't guarantee that the 20-year-old will remain with the Billy Goats long term, with Sport Bild reporting that a fresh bidding war for the German international could be on the cards in January.

Following recent reports from France suggesting that Paris Saint-Germain view El Mala as a potential replacement for the long-term injured Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Sport Bild claims that PSG had already approached 1. FC Köln sporting managing director Thomas Kessler about the youngster last summer.

No formal enquiry has been made at this stage, but PSG – along with several other clubs – are expected to keep a close eye on El Mala's development over the coming months.

The winger also remains on the radar of clubs in England, with Brighton & Hove Albion recently linked with a fresh approach.

Köln are understood to have put a higher price on El Mala since the summer, with Sport Bild suggesting that €50 million would no longer be enough to convince them to sell.

“You should never categorically rule anything out in football. He didn't extend his contract again without reason. Therefore, I currently see no reason to concern myself with a potential January move,” Köln sporting managing director Thomas Kessler told Sport Bild.

“I certainly don't need to tie Saïd down. He's a great lad who simply loves playing football. He feels very comfortable within the team, and I get the impression that he is growing increasingly attached to the club and everything around it.”

El Mala has scored four goals and provided one assist in nine appearances for Köln so far this season. He made his senior debut for Germany in October.

#2429. Feyenoord stretch lead ahead of Eredivisie top clash against PSV

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Feyenoord have opened up a three-point lead at the top of the Eredivisie ahead of next weekend’s clash with PSV, following the defending champions’ shock defeat at ADO Den Haag.

The Rotterdammers were made to work for their points in a seven-goal thriller at Telstar.

They took the lead after just 25 seconds when Gaoussou Diarra finished off a sweeping move and were 3-1 up after 32 minutes when Sem Steijn profited from good combination work by Gjivai Zechiël and Givairo Read.

Patrick Brouwer reduced the deficit five minutes later, but a second-half penalty by Steijn proved to be enough despite Noach Shenkman scoring a third for Telstar on 69 minutes.

Peter Bosz refused to blame the last-minute defeat at ADO on his injury crisis as he looks ahead to a testing week, with a trip to Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday followed by the visit of Feyenoord on Sunday.

PSV looked to be on course for a routine win when Sven Mijnans put them ahead in the 21st minute. But the midfielder’s dismissal just before half-time triggered a second-half collapse that culminated in Matej Sin’s headed winner for ADO in the 93rd minute.

Mijnans, who played as a makeshift striker, will be suspended for the game against Feyenoord, while Guus Til also went off after complaining of blurred vision after landing hard on his neck in the first half and is doubtful for the next week.

But Bosz said he did not fear his team was sliding into a “tricky situation” in the absence of other senior players such as Jerdy Schouten, Ricardo Pepi and new signing Sami Ouaissa.

“This is another chance to win a game,” he said. “Stick our chests out and not think in fear.”

AZ Alkmaar also dropped points against a newly promoted club as they could only draw 2-2 with Cambuur Leeuwarden even after the Friesland club lost Devid Bouah to a second yellow card early in the second half.

Twente Enschede missed the chance to leap into second place as Spanish striker Ángel Alarcón scored two superb goals for Utrecht to lift Anthony Correia’s team to 11th place.

Julian Brandt and Jorthy Mokio both scored twice as Ajax won 5-2 in Groningen in a match that saw both goalkeepers save penalties.

A double by Anthony Descotte looked to have earned Fortuna Sittard the points at NEC until Willum Thór Willumsson popped up with an injury-time header to snatch a draw for the struggling Nijmegen club.

#2428. Derek McInnes will need to do more than 'win ugly' if he is to thrive as Rangers manager

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 13:55 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:39 EDT, 1 November 2026

There have been several Rangers managers over the past ten years or so who never quite seemed to grasp the most basic and fundamental parameters of the job.

You either win matches and win trophies, or you are deemed a failure. If you do not fulfil that remit, there is no mitigation that can be offered. No extra points for artistic merit.

It is a reality which never felt like it sat all that comfortably with the likes of Mark Warburton, Michael Beale, Philippe Clement, Russell Martin or Danny Rohl.

Derek McInnes has spoken repeatedly this season about the fact that winning matches is ultimately what underpins everything else.

Unlike many of his predecessors, McInnes knows what is expected of him, and he knows what will and will not be tolerated by supporters.

Even on days when his team do not play overly well and it turns into a grind, as was the case in this Premier Sports Cup semi-final against Aberdeen at Hampden yesterday, getting the win is all that matters.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes enjoys his team's Premier Sports Cup victory over Aberdeen

Rangers fans have never demanded silky free-flowing football. Even Walter Smith’s nine-in-a-row team would never be mistaken for prime Barcelona. But they were efficient, effective and relentless.

But here’s the rub. Rangers are too often a tough watch at the moment. Winning ugly is a valuable and necessary trait to have for any manager in the Ibrox hotseat, no question.

When it starts to become the default method, however, it becomes more of a concern. This is where McInnes is still searching for the right balance in this Rangers team.

In the early part of the season, he flip-flopped between various different systems: 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1, 3-5-2, before eventually settling on 4-4-2.

Perhaps it was the back-to-back victories over Celtic in September that cemented in his own mind the belief that 4-4-2 would be the way forward.

But there have been times recently when it has looked an awkward fit. It didn’t work at all against Hearts at Tynecastle last week as Rangers scraped a 2-2 draw.

And, despite eventually grinding Aberdeen into submission courtesy of a late winner from Ryan Naderi, it didn’t really work yesterday.

Aberdeen arrived short-handed, with five defenders missing through injury or suspension, and set up to make the evening as awkward as possible for Rangers.

By and large, Stephen Robinson’s side succeeded in doing exactly that. It was a performance which offered some signs of life despite their woeful form in the league.

But the reality for Robinson heading into next weekend’s home clash with Hibs is that he probably needs a win in order to save his job.

Aberdeen will also rue a massive opportunity that was squandered by Kevin Nisbet on 76 minutes when the score was locked at 0-0.

After Stuart Armstrong fed a pass into his path, Nisbet hesitated when the situation demanded that he hit it first time.

Striker Ryan Naderi celebrates with supporters after scoring the only goal of the semi-final

Rangers dominated possession and had 25 shots at goal, although the fact that only five of those were on target was described as ‘embarrassing’ by McInnes.

But it was often slow and disjointed. As was the case at Tynecastle, they completely bypassed midfield and went long to Naderi and his strike partner Kevin Kelsy, looking to then play off second balls.

You wonder what might be possible from this Rangers team if they were to go with three in midfield and really control games properly and play through the lines.

It’s not like they don’t have the personnel. Nico Raskin and Dan Neil are more than capable of getting the ball down and playing football.

But the overall balance of the midfield just doesn’t look right at present. Perhaps this was why McInnes tried to shake things up by dropping Neil and playing James Penrice in the middle of the pitch at Hampden.

RANGERS (4-4-2): Pandur 6.5; Sterling 5, Fernandez 6.5 (Godfrey 89), Makhanya 7.5, Rommens 6 (Neil 65); BOUANANI 7.5 (Curtis 89), Penrice 7, Raskin 6, Min-su 6 (Gassama 65); Naderi 7.5, Kelsy 6.5 (Chukwuani 89).

ABERDEEN (3-5-2): Muller 7; Devlin 6.5 (Marshall 89), Molloy 6.5, Milne 6.5; Gyamfi 3 (Armstrong 14), Ronan 6 (Smith 89), Lyons 6.5, Aremu 7 (Yogane 89), Guinness-Walker 7.5; Nisbet 4, Mouloua 5 (Ntelo 56).

Penrice, a left-back by trade, didn’t have a poor game by any stretch. After eventually reverting to his normal position when Neil came off the bench, he teed up the winner for Naderi.

But, playing him in midfield was a change that never really worked. It was a square peg in a round hole – and actually highlighted the lack of faith that McInnes has in some players.

Tochi Chukwuani and Vanja Dragojevic were signed for a total outlay of almost £9million. Chukwuani hasn’t started a game since the defeat to Jablonec and has been limited to substitute appearances.

Dragojevic also hasn’t featured from the start since the Jablonec game – and has made only one substitute appearance since then.

The word from Rangers is that the 20-year-old midfielder, who captained Partizan Belgrade, is a talent but still very raw. That’s fine. But he is not going to develop if he doesn’t play any football.

Chukwuani and Dragojevic were both signed for good money. The current system has cast them as bystanders. It is incumbent on McInnes as manager to nurture that talent.

All in all, this was an exercise in winning ugly for Rangers. There is, of course, a lot to be said for that. Especially in cup semi-finals, getting the job done is all that matters.

But when winning ugly starts to become the norm rather than a fallback, it is only natural that fans will start to question the style of play.

Badredine Bouanani was Rangers’ best player against Aberdeen. He was a constant menace to them, cutting in from the right on to his left foot.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet could not come up with the goal his team needed at Hampden

Minsu Kim probably had his poorest game yet in a Rangers jersey. But there’s no doubting his talent and the fact he’s a player around whom things should be built this season.

Ultimately, McInnes is still searching for the right balance. That search is visible in the selections and in the way the team plays.

A midfield that can control the tempo, progress the ball cleanly through pressure, and offer both defensive cover and creative outlets remains a work in progress.

This victory at Hampden demonstrated the progress being made in terms of a team who can grind it out, but also highlighted some of the limitations that remain in this Rangers team.

Winning ugly is a useful habit. Whether it can evolve into something more fluent on a consistent basis remains to be seen.

Whether midfielders purchased at considerable expense can be integrated rather than left on the periphery, and whether the long-ball tendency becomes a Plan B to fall back on or merely the default style of play – these are the issues that will define how this Rangers team develops under McInnes.

#2426. England’s Dutch coach Sarina Wiegman extends contract until 2029

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch football coach Sarina Wiegman has extended her contract with the England women’s team by two years, taking her up to the 2029 European Championships.

Wiegman, 56, led the team to two European titles in 2022 and 2025, as well as their first World Cup final in 2023, when they lost to Spain.

Prior to that she won the European Championships with the Dutch national team in 2017 and reached the World Cup final two years later, losing 2-0 to the United States.

“I am so happy to be able to carry on with this squad and cannot think of a better job in football,” she said in a statement released by the English Football Association (FA).

“Working for a world-class organisation like the FA, and alongside so many people dedicated to winning England teams and the growth of our game, excites me every day.”

FA chief executive Mark Bullingham described Wiegman as “an incredible coach with an unparalleled record in major tournaments”. He added: “There is no one better to lead the Lionesses into the next two tournaments.”

Commentators had widely expected the Dutchwoman to leave her post after next year’s World Cup, after England failed to qualify automatically for the tournament.

A 4-0 loss to Spain in June, the team’s heaviest defeat since Wiegman took charge, means they will have to come through a play-off tournament with Greece, Ukraine and Slovakia to reach the finals in Brazil.

Wiegman said: “Anyone who knows me will understand that my main concern right now is absolutely the World Cup, and helping this squad realise their potential in the years to come.

“We have an important job to do to confirm our place in Brazil, and hopefully we can do that and give the country another special summer to remember next year.”

#2424. Falkirk boss John McGlynn backs Scott Bain to be Scotland's No 1 after 'game of his life' against Celtic

Published: 14:59 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:59 EDT, 1 November 2026

Falkirk manager John McGlynn has backed goalkeeper Scott Bain to establish himself as Scotland's No1 between the sticks after producing the 'game of his life' to earn his side a stunning 2-0 win over Celtic.

Bain has been in top form this season, and was at his very best once again as he pulled off a string of outstanding stops to keep the defending champions at bay, with Ethan Ross and Scott Tanser finding the net for Falkirk at the other end.

The 34-year-old was called into new national team boss Sebastien Pocognoli's squad for the recent Nations League quadruple-header, but had to settle for a place on the bench, with Angus Gunn given the nod.

But McGlynn believes the former Celtic shot-stopper has done more than enough to earn an opportunity to add to his four Scotland caps when the next round of international fixtures comes around later this month.

He said: 'I don't want to take anything away from the outfield players but Scott Bain had the game of his life.

'I've been pushing Scotty for a while because I know how good and calm and good with his feet he is.

Scott Bain acknowledges the Falkirk supporters after his stunning display against Celtic

Falkirk boss John McGlynn says keeper Bain had the 'game of his life' in their 2-0 victory

Bain pulls off one of several fine saves by turning Haissem Hassan's shot round the post

'Everything you want he'll deliver. Wherever you are, he can't go unnoticed. He could easily be doing a job for Celtic but I'm delighted we've got him and he's producing the goods which can only help us going forwards.'

McGlynn was delighted with his side's overall display which delivered a fourth Premiership victory on the bounce.

The Bairns are now up to fourth in the table, and have the chance to leapfrog Hearts next weekend when they take the trip to Tynecastle.

'Huge credit to my players,' he said. 'It was a remarkable shift.

'It was a great start. To get a goal so early is beyond your wildest dreams because you're usually chasing the game.

'We defended well and defended set plays and he [Bain] was there to save or punch.

'There was [good] football in there. It was a great second goal and Scotty [Tanser] hasn't been in the mix and hasn't played a lot.

'For him to come in and have the calmness to slot it away... I'm delighted. There's a great opportunity for him on that side.

'Huge compliments to every player. The subs had to go on and continue what the players had been doing which was working really hard and they did that.

'Four wins on the bounce, three clean sheets in a row. Ecstatic.

'The boys have been doing great in these weeks. We've had some sore ones losing late goals.

'There's been a togetherness that's taken us to another rung of the ladder and they've gone the extra mile for each other. Today will increase our determination and desire to get better.

'It's been building. There were signs. We've been in every game.

'It's going to give them a huge boost. At the start we had some big fixtures which is difficult when you're putting a team together.

'We had the confidence going into this game and we'll go to Tynecastle with a lot of confidence, [but] Hearts have been exceptional there.'

The win was Falkirk's first in ten fixtures against either half of the Old Firm since their return to the top flight last summer, and the manager admitted he was pleased to finally get the monkey off their back.

'It was one of the boxes left to tick,' he said. 'Thankfully we've done that.

'Last season over 24 points against the Old Firm we got two, when we drew with Rangers twice, so we're already a point better off. Hopefully there are more points to pick up.'

PSV survived a second-half onslaught in Porto to secure their first win of the Champions League group stages.

The Eindhoven club were worth their narrow lead against Francesco Farioli’s side after dominating possession in the first half, but rarely troubled Diogo Costa in the Porto goal.

At the other end, substitute Denis Man came close to scoring a second for PSV with his first touch when his curling shot beat Costa but failed to sneak inside the post.

The 1-0 win lifts PSV to a provisional 16th place in the Champions League table at the halfway stage of round three, while Porto are still looking for their first point.

Their next match is at home to Belgian side Club Brugge, who will make the short trip to Eindhoven on November 4.

#2420. After Robbie Fowler claimed the moon landing is 'bulls***' and dubious Joe Cole said he has 'questions' for Neil Armstrong... who makes our ultimate XI of football conspiracy theorists?

Published: 02:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:15 EDT, 1 November 2026

Robbie Fowler certainly helped to draw attention to his new podcast with his former Liverpool and England team-mate Steve McManaman this week by airing his views on the 1969 moon landing.

After answering fan questions ranging from favourite films, comedians and useless talents, Fowler responded to McManaman's prompt of the moon landing as a conspiracy theory.

'I think the moon landing is bulls*** to be fair,' with an excited McManaman declaring 'that is a massive one,' before declaring his subsequent reasoning made 'perfect sense'.

He is far from the only footballer to have doubts, with another ex-England international Joe Cole declaring he would like to sit down with Neil Armstrong – who died in 2012 – to get to the bottom of it.

Fowler later quipped he is 'not a flat earther' having been up on a plane. However, some former footballers are, while others have raised a wide range of conspiracies, ranging from the small scale to the more wild.

Here, Daily Mail Sport puts together our ultimate XI of football's conspiracy theorists.

Former Liverpool forward Robbie Fowler admitted this week he believes the moon landing is 'bulls***' Source: YouTube - We'll have a look podcast

For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist – so entrenched in his off-the-wall beliefs and so willing to share them publicly that he is more widely known as a crackpot than a goalkeeper.

Nevertheless, Icke turned out for Coventry City's youth set-up between the sticks in the late 1960s, and later played for semi-professional outfit Hereford United before hanging up his boots and pivoting to sports journalism.

While his playing career might have been small-fry, his commitment to conspiracy theories is Premier League. Among his often-cited beliefs is the idea that an inter-dimensional race of reptile-like shape-shifters – the 'Babylon Brotherhood' have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society.

Among the accused are the late Queen Mother, the Rockefeller and Rothschild families, and former Prime Minister Edward Heath, whose eyes, Icke alleged, he saw turn 'jet black' when the pair met in 1989.

Icke also believes that the 'Illuminati' at the top of the global food chain organised world events including Dunblane, 9/11, the assassination of John F Kennedy, the death of Princess Diana to prompt their subsequent responses. Less laughable is the thick seam of anti-Semitism which critics believe runs through his thinking, although Icke has denied this.

For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist, with one of his cited beliefs is the idea that reptile-like shape-shifters have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society

Javi Poves endured a similarly unmemorable professional playing career in Spain, but did at least register one La Liga appearance with Sporting Gijon. Then, he quit. It was a matter of principle: he had grown to believe that 'professional football is only money and corruption'. Not an unreasonable view point, from some perspectives, but years on from his 2011 resignation things become somewhat more surreal.

Poves joined lower-division Madrid club Mostoles Balompie in 2016 and later became the club's president. In 2019, he renamed the club Flat Earth FC, to draw attention to his primary cause.

'Football is the most popular sport and has the most impact worldwide, so creating a club dedicated to the flat earth movement is the best way to have a constant presence in the media,' he said that year.

'Flat Earth FC is the first football club whose followers are united by the most important thing, which is an idea.'

Although Poves has since moved to fellow amateur side CDC Moscardo, he remains passionately committed to the idea that the earth is flat and not round, and other environmentally-rooted conspiracy theories. These include viewing 'chemtrails' as a deployment of toxic chemicals, and refusing to believe that suncream can help prevent skin cancer.

One thread which runs through a number of players included in the XI is a scepticism of Covid-19. Some, like Sol Campbell, have suggested that the pandemic was in some way man-made. Icke is in the camp which believes that the lockdown and vaccination scheme was akin to governmental 'facism'.

Lovren was firmly in team Icke during the lockdown years, posting a number of his videos on social media. He also used social media to attack Microsoft billionaire Bill Gates, implying some kind of conspiracy with his comment: 'Game over Bill. People are not blind' on Gates's online tribute to health workers.

The Croatian defender seemed particularly swayed by Icke's theories around the links between Covid-19 and 5G technology in 'controlling' populations, with Lovren resharing clips with the caption 'we will not be censored'.

Dejan Lovren supported Icke's views during the pandemic and hit out at Bill Gates

Lovren took to Instagram to promote an interview with Icke during the pandemic

As mentioned in Lovren's section, Campbell also had his suspicions during the Covid-19 pandemic. Then managing Southend United, in May 2020, Campbell appeared to suggest that he believed the disease was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups.

'Was this virus a natural mistake or a designed mistake...?' he posted on social media. 'I wonder does this virus deliberately attacks a certain blood type.....?'

Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group. He later was widely derided for having no scientific evidence to support his argument.

Sol Campbell appeared to suggest in 2020 he believed Covid-`9 was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups

Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group

The former Manchester City defender has previously admitted to a conspiracy theory that has more sympathetic readers nodding in approval: he believes in ghosts.

Delph admitted in 2016 that he sees ghosts 'all the time', adding that 'genuinely' he had seen about 'four'.

'When I first signed for (Aston) Villa I stayed in a hotel there was lots of things moving in the room, a lot of bangs,' he told Man City's official YouTube channel.

'And about four months ago I saw, in my house in God's country (Yorkshire), I saw two ghosts in my bedroom.'

'I don't think they're there to harm me. But I've definitely seen them. It was just a split second and then they were gone.

'The one four months ago, that actually was carrying a body, it went out onto my balcony, then disappeared.'

Joe Cole admitted he is open to having his head turnedabout the moon landings and would be keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong to 'get to the bottom of things'

Compared to how some of the other members of Daily Mail Sport's XI have at times risked public safety or aired unpleasant and divisive views, Cole's position on the 1969 Moon Landings feels somewhat milquetoast.

Additionally, unlike many, he admitted that he is open to having his head turned, with Cole keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong, the first man on the moon, to 'get to the bottom' of things.

'I'm not sold either way and I need some convincing. I want to believe it, honestly,' Cole told FourFourTwo. 'But I've heard too much about it being fake - things like the flag waving and the footprints and all the rest of it.

'I would love to sit down with a man who actually went there and be convinced. I want him to tell me exactly how it all went down and some of the science behind my questions.

'I just want to put it to bed. If anyone could convince me, it's the first man to have apparently visited the moon. I don't mind being talked round to new ideas which is why I'd be more than happy for him to tell me how silly I'm being.

'That's what makes you evolve as a human being. You have to be open to different ideas in life.'

If Pove represents a distinctly Spanish-style conspiracy theorist, Marcos Llorente treads the well-beaten path, with his primary focus the benefits of sunlight – to the extent of snubbing suncream – and a suspicion of 'chemtrails'.

Llorente takes his theories on natural light and the sun to the extreme, however. A staunch advocate of the blue light-blocking sunglasses also favoured by stars including Erling Haaland, the Atletico Madrid midfielder also eschews unnatural light sources in his house after dark. Instead, Llorente works on soaking up as much red light as possible.

In the sun, Llorente takes it one step further, frequently sharing incorrect views on suncream's impact on Vitamin D and dismissing the connection between skin cancer and unprotected skin.

Marcos Llorente is a committed wearer of blue light-blocking glasses in a bid to boost his melatonin

Llorente has frequently endorsed the repeatedly debunked theory that 'chemtrails' are the result of government or corporate intervention

Llorente often does so in a tongue-in-cheek way: in April, he dressed up as a bottle of suncream, but with a twist. Written on the bottle in Spanish were messages reading: 'Protect against your biology' and 'Blocking Vitamin D since 1985'.

On the back of the bottle costume in lieu of ingredients, Llorente drew a graph of rising skin cancer rates and an accompanying message.

'Get in the shade when your body tells you, 'That's enough'. Get sun exposure year-round, not just three days in August,' the 'warning label' read. 'Use clothing as sun protection. Start in the morning and work your way up (don't start at 1pm).

'Build melanin gradually. Eat a balanced diet so your skin responds better. Stay hydrated and connect with nature.'

More recently Llorente, a bon viveur and lover of rare steak, 'bulletproof' butter coffee and good wine, has intensified his stance on other medical theories, including alleging that high cholesterol or 'bad' cholesterol does not have an impact on health.

Matt Le Tissier is no single-issue conspiracy theorist, with the Southampton icon borderline indiscriminate about the wide range of his causes.

Like many, his outpourings amplified amid the pandemic, with Le Tissier frequently opining on the efficacy of vaccines and painting 'big pharma' as a bogeyman. Then, in 2022, he was stood down from his role as Saints ambassador after peddling Russian lies that the massacre at Bucha, in Ukraine, had been fabricated. This came despite the fact that there was video, satellite, and photographic evidence that Russia had murdered over 320 people in the town.

Earlier this year, Le Tissier found himself in a spat with Grok, X's AI chatbot, over 'chemtrails', asking: 'Hey (Grok), why do some plane trails disperse quickly while others hang around and spread out to form grey blanket clouds?'

The bot had responded that the contrails lingered or didn't due to atmospheric conditions, much to Le Tissier's displeasure, with the former midfielder grumbling that Grok was 'spouting government propaganda'.

Matt Le Tissier, pictured taking a selfie at a Southampton game in February, has frequently raised conspiracy theories over social media

Former Wales international David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas.

Cotterill said in the incendiary post that 'false flag events are one of their go to methods of manipulating the public opinion to bring about change'.

He also alleged: 'America is the last major country that allows it's [sic] citizens to arm themselves. Which they can't really have with what they're planning to do in the coming months and years.'

Cotterill later stressed that the post had not been related to the Texas massacre, instead stating that his post was 'just about recent articles when you see some of the stuff about the pandemic'.

He similarly received intense criticism when he suggested that the retirement of Brighton's 24-year-old Enock Mwepu due to cardiac issues was linked to side effect of the Covid-19 vaccine.

Cotterill remains unrepentant however, recently appearing on a podcast where he admitted that he supports 'everything' Le Tissier says, and revealed his belief in 2016's discredited Pizzagate conspiracy, among other conspiracy theories.

'I've gone into so many rabbit holes. If you see lots of things happening in the world with the number 33, which is obviously massive for Freemasonry and symbolism,' he told Made in Brum Podcast. 'If you see a lot of things that happen in the world, 33 is not far from that. Some people think I'm f***ing nuts.

David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas

Former Liverpool and Southampton star Rickie Lambert is among this cohort's Covid-19 conspiracy theorists, starting off on social media as a staunch vaccine sceptic - only to fall deeper into more fringe views.

Unusually, in 2023, Lambert claimed that he believed that one can change the molecular structure of water based on speaking to a glass of the substance positively or negatively.

'The one word where water responds in the most beautiful way, with the most beautiful crystals, is showing gratitude to water,' Lambert said.

More recently, Lambert has been an active supporter of the campaign against '15-minute cities', whose detractors believe is a government scheme to control the movement and rights of people, rather than an attempt to provide walkable goods and services.

Ahead of attending a protest in Liverpool in September 2023, Lambert's call to arms to publicise the event stressed that the scheme was 'a controlled tactic being implemented across this country' and that Merseyside was set to be put under permanent surveillance.

Rickie Lambert has claimed talking positively to water makes it clean

Like Cole, Fowler appears to have merely dipped a toe into the world of conspiratorial thinking, and has similarly alighted on the Moon Landing as the target of his suspicion.

Unlike the former Chelsea star however, there seemed to be little that would change his mind when he discussed the topic with his We'll Have A Look podcast with co-host Steve McManaman.

'I think the Moon Landing is bulls***, to be fair,' Fowler said. 'Because there was a race in the Sixties, between the Americans and the USSR.

'All of a sudden, the USSR were ahead of the Americans (after Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space) and all of a sudden, the Americans got there first.

'I think it's a bit far-fetched. I don't know, that is the general gist of what I'm saying - I just don't think it was real.'
